primary_outcome: The CNN predicts the effective thermal conductivity of a 128x128 two-phase image in 15 ms, which the abstract calls 3 to 5 orders of magnitude faster than the finite-volume simulation that each iteration of the voxel-swap topology optimization would otherwise need.
outcome_location: Abstract (first quantitative comparison with a classical method); the same comparison is elaborated with exact numbers in Sec. 4.2 (CPU-vs-CPU, Table 1) and Sec. 5.1-5.4 (GPU-based per-iteration speed-ups inside the topology-optimization case studies)
R1_evidence_with_locators: The primary outcome is a per-evaluation comparison (abstract; Sec. 4.2, p. 7), and at that level the CNN is checked against the same NHT solver it replaces: test MAPE 0.35-2.35% on 26,000 held-out images per conductivity ratio (Table 5, Fig. 5, p. 7), plus the analytical parallel and series cases (Sec. 4.3). The comparison therefore sits within the ML method's reported error of the classical result, as in adjudicated record P00149. In the optimization application the CNN- and NHT-driven variants share the voxel-swap and simulated-annealing optimizer and the budget of 1,000,000 attempts (Sec. 5, p. 7), and every accepted CNN swap is re-evaluated by NHT (Figs. 7-10). The NHT-driven run itself was only extrapolated (102,778 h), not executed.
R2_evidence_with_locators: The state equation (2D steady-state heat conduction) is elliptic, matching R2's scope. The classical NHT solver uses TDMA line-sweeps applied iteratively (not a sparse direct solve of the full system nor a multigrid-preconditioned Krylov method), and Table 1 reports 32,903-154,307 iterations to converge a single 16,384-cell (128x128) image -- a very large iteration count for a linear 2D Poisson-type problem of this size, consistent with the partial condition 'the implementation looks inefficient... but no direct comparison is possible' (no re-test is performed in this coding pass, so R2(a)/(e) cannot be checked directly). Problem size (16,384 DOFs) is below the 10^5-DOF threshold named in R2(c), so the GPU (CNN, RTX 3070) vs. CPU (NHT, Bridges2 cores) asymmetry does not trigger an automatic fail, but it is also not justified in the article, and the CPU-vs-CPU claim in Sec. 4.2 ('using one CPU core, the CNN is 3 to 5 orders of magnitude faster') reuses Table 1's NHT times without confirming they came from the same CPU model (Ryzen 7 3700X) used for the CNN's own CPU benchmark. Re-test pointer for (a)/(e): a sparse direct or multigrid solve of the same 128x128 finite-volume system on one core, compared with the 34.2-371.2 s per image of Table 1.
R3_evidence_with_locators: Data-generation cost is reported concretely: 520,000 NHT simulations on a named supercomputer resource (Bridges2; Sec. 1, 2.3), with per-image times in Table 1 from which a total core-time is directly derivable. Training cost is reported concretely: about 1 hour per model on one HPC node with 4 NVIDIA V100 GPUs for 600 epochs (Sec. 4.2). The Conclusion (Sec. 6) explicitly states the cost relationship between them ('training of the CNN itself is minuscule... compared to creating a large dataset'), and every headline speed figure in Sec. 4.2 and Sec. 5 is explicitly scoped to per-image / per-iteration / per-batch inference, i.e. the claim is explicitly limited to per-query cost with both upstream costs disclosed rather than hidden.
R4_evidence_with_locators: The returned designs of all four optimization runs, and every accepted swap on the way, are re-evaluated with the NHT finite-volume model and compared with the closed-form bounds (Sec. 5.1-5.4, Figs. 7-10, pp. 8-9). The porosity of 0.5 is kept exactly by the one-for-one swap rule (Sec. 5, p. 7), and all four runs are reported, none selected. Solid-phase connectivity is not a constraint of this two-phase conduction problem: Sec. 5.4 treats the checkerboard as the admissible maximum-surface-area state [judgment]. The CNN predictions are also shown against NHT for all 26,000 test images (Fig. 5), not only as averages. No unreported constraint violation or failure count is evident; unsure means pass.

authors: Martin Eigel, Marvin Haase, Johannes Neumann
title: Topology Optimisation under Uncertainties with Neural Networks
venue: Algorithms 15(7), 241 (MDPI; published 12 July 2022; open access, CC BY)
reason: I-SPEED (screening code confirmed at full text)
primary_outcome: Deterministic 2D bridge, nominal load: inserting CNN-predicted gradient steps every 55 iterations cut convergence from 538 to 441 iterations, with lower compliance (1148.66 vs 1173.22) and run time 4 min 05 s vs 4 min 43 s.
outcome_location: Sec. 4.1.3, Table 1 (p. 22): first quantitative comparison with the classical optimizer (iterations, J, compliance); the matching times are in Table 4 (p. 28). The abstract, conclusion and introduction compare only qualitatively
R1_evidence_with_locators: Tables 1 and 4: both optimizers solve the same problem with the same volume constraint (m = 0.4) and the same convergence criterion (Eq. A1), and the CNN-assisted design has lower J and compliance at the nominal load, so the time gain (4 min 05 s vs 4 min 43 s) does not come with worse quality. Achieved volumes are not reported. For two of five loads (Table 4) the CNN design is about 0.6% worse in compliance [derived] while faster; a verifier who weighs those cases may choose partial.
R2_evidence_with_locators: Sec. 4 and App. B: the baseline is the authors' own phase-field optimizer (refs [1,2]) in the same FEniCS code, and the NN steps are inserted into the same loop, so implementation and hardware are shared [inferred]; hardware and linear solver are not stated. The mesh has up to about 15,000 vertices [≈3×10⁴ DOFs, derived], so (c) does not apply; (b) not observed (no figure in the abstract); (d) not applicable (convergence-based stopping). A per-iteration time is derivable (283 s ÷ 538 ≈ 0.53 s, adaptive mesh [derived]), but the phase-field gradient flow differs from a SIMP strong baseline, so (e) is hard to apply. Unsure, so pass.
R3_evidence_with_locators: Sec. 4.1.1 and 4.2.1: the networks are trained on sample paths of the classical optimizer (S runs with random load rotations, up to 500 iterations each), but S, the data-generation time and the training time are not reported, and no break-even is given. The claim is not limited to per-query use. For C3: the saving is about 38 s per run at the nominal load (Table 4) [derived], so each training path (about one classical run [inferred]) needs roughly 7 uses to pay back [derived].
R4_evidence_with_locators: Tables 1-4: J and compliance come from the FE state solve of the converged designs, which continue with classical steps after each NN step [inferred]. Achieved volume is not reported. Topology collapse for an unsuitable insertion interval c_m or for loads far from the training data is described only qualitatively (Sec. 4.1.4, 4.4), with no counts. The extra loads are a hand-picked selection of extreme cases (three in Sec. 4.1.4 and Table 3; a fourth appears only in Table 4).

authors: Abid Ullah, Karim Asami, Lukas Holtz, Tim Röver, Kashif Azher, Katharina Bartsch, Claus Emmelmann
title: A Machine Learning Approach for Mechanical Component Design Based on Topology Optimization Considering the Restrictions of Additive Manufacturing
venue: Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing 8(5), 220 (MDPI; published 1 October 2024; CC BY 4.0)
primary_outcome: A Pix2Pix cGAN replaces iterative ToPy SIMP runs (about 90 s each) with millisecond generation for a parameterized 100×100 cantilever; up to 91% of test outputs are artefact-free, judged only by pixel comparison with the TO images.
outcome_location: Abstract (eliminating the iterative TO steps; 91% reliability), Sec. 1 and Sec. 2.2 p. 6 (90 s per ToPy run vs milliseconds); 91% also in Sec. 3.1 and Sec. 6
R1_evidence_with_locators: Secs. 1, 2.2, 3.1 and 3.2: millisecond ML generation is set against complete 70-iteration ToPy runs (about 90 s), while the ML outputs are measurably worse: 9% (Models 3-4) to over 50% (Model 6) of test outputs have artefacts or unconnected structures. Quality is compared only by pixel deviation, with no compliance evaluation (Sec. 3.2), and no equal-quality or equal-time matching is attempted.
R2_evidence_with_locators: Secs. 2.1-2.2: ToPy (Python SIMP, solver not stated) with a fixed 70 iterations took about 90 s per 100×100 design on an unnamed 12-core CPU at 25% utilization, about 1.29 s per iteration [derived]. Our strong baseline's median per-iteration time on a larger 256×256 cantilever (6.5 times more elements) is 0.336 s with PARDISO (retest/logs/g2_benchmark_2026-09-24.log), already 3.8 times faster [derived]; at 100×100 the gap is likely at least 10 times [inferred], so R2(e) needs our re-test at this size. (b), (c) and (d) are not established: about 2×10^4 DOFs, and 70 fixed iterations with a stated change criterion.
R3_evidence_with_locators: Sec. 2.2: data generation is reported (250 h serial, 62.5 h with four concurrent runs, for 10,000 pairs) and called a one-time cost, but training time is not reported and no break-even is given. For C3: the data alone cost the CPU time of 10,000 classical runs, so the model must serve at least 10,000 designs to recoup it, before training cost [derived].
R4_evidence_with_locators: Sec. 3.2: validation is limited to pixel-by-pixel comparison with the ToPy images plus visual inspection, and the authors state that FEM validation was not performed. Artefact and disconnection counts are reported (Sec. 3.1), but no returned design is evaluated for compliance or volume.
